opus-5.5.text:
I'd point to a few moments that, looking back, gradually turned embodied AI from a niche corner of robotics into something people treat as a central question for AI.

The first was the deep learning revolution itself, around 2012 with ImageNet and AlexNet. That wasn't embodied AI, but it showed that learning from data could beat hand-engineered pipelines in perception. Right after that, people in robotics started asking: if vision can be learned end to end, can action be learned too? Work around 2015 and 2016 on end-to-end visuomotor policies, and the large-scale grasping experiments where many robot arms collected data in parallel, planted that seed.

The second was AlphaGo and the rise of deep reinforcement learning. It convinced many people that agents could learn complex behavior through interaction, not just from labeled data. A wave of researchers then took RL into simulation, things like locomotion and manipulation, and simulation platforms and benchmarks for embodied navigation and interaction made "embodied AI" an actual research community with shared tasks, rather than scattered robotics projects.

But I think the real turning point was large language models, especially after ChatGPT at the end of 2022. Two things happened at once. First, people saw what a general-purpose model could do, and the natural next question was: language and the digital world are only half of intelligence, so what about the physical world? Second, LLMs and vision-language models gave robots a kind of common-sense brain for the first time: understanding instructions, planning tasks, recognizing open-vocabulary objects. Work that connected these models to robot actions, the vision-language-action line of research, made it concrete. You could see a path from foundation models to robots.

Then there's the hardware and industry side. Humanoid robots became much more capable and much cheaper over the past few years, especially with China's supply chain for motors, reducers and batteries maturing so quickly. When major tech companies and many startups, including us at Galbot, committed seriously to general-purpose robots, capital and talent flowed in. In China, embodied AI also became a national priority, which accelerated things further.

So if I had to summarize: deep learning made learning-based robotics plausible, deep RL and simulation built the research community, foundation models gave robots a brain and gave the field a clear vision of generality, and hardware maturity plus industrial investment made it real. Embodied AI is now seen as the bridge from digital intelligence to physical intelligence, and many people, myself included, think it's essential for truly general AI.

That said, I'd caution that we haven't had our "ChatGPT moment" yet. The core bottleneck is still data: there's no internet-scale corpus of physical interaction. How we solve that, whether through synthetic data and simulation, large-scale teleoperation, or learning from human video, will likely define the next milestone.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, because I think the field didn't arrive through one single moment, it came in waves, and each wave shifted what people believed was possible.

If I go back a bit, the first thing I'd point to is actually from the vision side rather than robotics. Around 2012, deep learning on ImageNet showed that perception could be learned end to end from data. For those of us working on 3D vision, that was the signal that if you had enough data, you could learn to understand the physical world, and understanding the world is the prerequisite for acting in it. A few years later, work like ShapeNet and the whole 3D object datasets movement extended that to geometry, and that's when my own interest really started to move from "seeing" to "seeing in order to manipulate."

The second wave is deep reinforcement learning. DeepMind's Atari results and then AlphaGo around 2016 made the idea of learning a policy, not just a classifier, feel real. On the robotics side, Google's arm farm and Sergey Levine's group showed you could learn grasping from large-scale real-world trials. OpenAI's dexterous hand solving a Rubik's cube in 2019 was, for me, a very important moment, because dexterous manipulation is the hardest part, and sim-to-real transfer with domain randomization suddenly seemed feasible. It also made simulation infrastructure a first-class topic, and things like Isaac Gym with GPU-parallel physics changed how fast a student could iterate.

The third wave, and this is the one that made "embodied AI" a term everyone uses, is large models. When ChatGPT came out at the end of 2022, people who had never cared about robots started asking, what's the equivalent of this for the physical world? Google's SayCan and then RT-1, RT-2 showed that you could connect language and vision models to robot actions, and the Open X-Embodiment effort showed that pooling data across many robots actually helps. That's when the idea of a "foundation model for robots" became a serious research program rather than a slogan.

And then I'd add a hardware and industry wave running in parallel. Tesla announcing Optimus, Figure, Unitree bringing humanoid and legged platforms to a price where university labs can afford them, and in China a very fast growth of companies around humanoids. Capital flowing in matters, because embodied AI is expensive. You need robots, you need data collection, you need people who can do both learning and mechanical engineering.

So if I had to compress it: ImageNet gave us learned perception, AlphaGo and the dexterous hand gave us learned control, ChatGPT and RT-2 gave us a common model backbone and the imagination that generalist robots are possible, and the humanoid hardware wave gave us the bodies to put it all in. The honest caveat I always give is that the data problem is still unsolved. Language models had the internet; robots don't have an internet of actions yet. How we build that, through simulation, teleoperation, or video, is really the question defining the field right now.

astra-6.text:
I’d say it was a progression rather than a single event. First, advances in computer vision and deep learning made it possible for machines to extract useful information from complex environments. Then reinforcement learning showed the potential for learning how to act, although much of that progress happened in games and simulation.

The emergence of large language models brought these directions closer together. It raised a compelling question: if a model can understand instructions and reason about a task, can we connect that ability to a robot that actually carries it out? Work linking vision, language, and action made that question much more concrete.

For me, the important shift is that physical interaction became central to the discussion of intelligence. A robot has to deal with the consequences of its actions, incomplete observations, and a world that doesn’t behave exactly as expected. That makes embodied AI both a practical challenge and an important way to investigate what intelligence requires.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d point to a few milestones rather than one single event. The first was the progress in deep learning that made visual perception much more capable. A robot needs to understand what is around it before it can act, so that was an important foundation.

Then reinforcement learning showed that machines could learn complex sequences of decisions. AlphaGo was a very visible example, although acting in the physical world is much harder than playing a game with clearly defined rules.

More recently, large language models brought much broader attention to the question: can we connect this kind of intelligence to perception and action? For me, that is the key transition. An embodied system has to turn an instruction into action, observe what actually happens, and adjust. The convergence of those capabilities is what has made embodied AI such an important field.
